title: What Theodore Roosevelt Can Teach Us About Being a Gentleman
author: Chris Martin
source: The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack), March 14, 2026
summary: Martin holds Theodore Roosevelt as a model of classical gentlemanhood despite (or because of) his bold public achievements. Roosevelt overcame severe childhood asthma through deliberate physical and mental discipline, developing a philosophy that true gentlemen confront hardship head-on rather than avoid it. Martin traces Roosevelt's courage (which appeared both on battlefields like San Juan Hill and in unpopular moral stands), his ability to combine strength with courtesy and restraint, and his commitment to the "strenuous life" of service and challenge rather than comfort. What emerges is Roosevelt as a template for modern gentlemen: one who builds strength in body and character, accepts responsibility and risk, speaks softly while carrying authority, and seeks service to something larger than himself.
points: Roosevelt overcame severe childhood asthma not through excuses but through relentless self-improvement in body, mind, and character—proving that a gentleman is forged through difficulty, not despite it.

True courage appears in both dramatic forms (leading a charge) and subtle ones (standing by unpopular principles)—a gentleman takes responsibility and accepts risks rather than criticizing from the sidelines.

The balance between strength and courtesy captures gentlemanhood: power without discipline becomes arrogance; courtesy without strength becomes weakness—Roosevelt's "speak softly and carry a big stick" captures this tension.
Roosevelt believed the biggest danger facing prosperous society is comfort, not hardship—character is forged through discipline, not convenience, a lesson all modern men should absorb.
Leadership is service and responsibility, not status or privilege—Roosevelt demonstrated noblesse oblige by using privilege and power on behalf of others, not himself.
quotes: Few men in American history embodied the ideals of courage and character as clearly as Theodore Roosevelt. Not only is he known for his achievements as President of the United States, he is remembered as the epitome of manliness and a strenuous life.

As a child, Roosevelt suffered from severe asthma and poor health. Doctors warned that he might never live a normal life. However, Roosevelt was not an ordinary child. He chose the opposite path. He began to build up his body with relentless determination.
Nothing in the world is worth having or worth doing unless it means effort, pain, difficulty. A man should deliberately build strength of body, mind, and character.
It is not the critic who counts… The credit belongs to the man who is actually in the arena. A gentleman does not waste time criticizing others from the sidelines.

One of the most striking qualities about Roosevelt was his ability to combine strength with courtesy. Even when he disagreed strongly with someone, he rarely lost his cool or became bitter towards them. Speak softly and carry a big stick.

I wish to preach, not the doctrine of ignoble ease, but the doctrine of the strenuous life. Character is not developed through comfort. It is forged through discipline and the willingness to take on difficult tasks.” Archived from The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
